pr_body: This PR adds the `extension create` command. It creates the local scaffolding for developing an extension and then outputs instructions on next steps for the user. Does not install the extension locally or publish the extension. Fixes https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/4104 Supersedes https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/4157
pr_comments: @vilmibm I addressed your comments, let me know what you think. I skipped adding a prompt for the extension name since none of the other `extension` commands use prompts and I wanted to keep it consistent.

issue_context.title: Add an `extension create` command
issue_context.body:
In the interest of helping people get going with extensions authorship, we'll add a command for initializing a new skeleton extension.

something like:

```bash
gh extension init

? New command name: echo
✓ Created directory gh-echo
✓ Initialized git repository
✓ Set up repository

gh-echo is ready for development.

Install locally with: gh extension install gh-repo

Publish to github with: gh repo create gh-repo

For more information on writing extensions: https://some.link/foobar 
```
comments: This is awesome, I'm excited! One nit, let's use create instead of init to stay consistent with our design patterns unless there's a compelling reason to depart from that.

> ```shell
> gh extension install gh-repo
> ```

Local extensions are only installable from a current directory `gh extension install .`, but not via another relative path. So I would propose first cd'ing into a directory and installing it there!

Should the `create` command install the new extension for you? I feel like it could, because you would most likely do it yourself soon after.

I'm fine with `create`.

regarding installing locally on their behalf, I want to make sure this is a teachable moment: if this is someone's first extension, it might also be their first time needing to install an extension locally.

If we do install it for them i want to be very clear about what commands we ran. I'll play around with both (documenting next steps vs. doing it for them with clear documentation) and see what feels better.
@samcoe is going to help out with this work

Thoughts regarding the scope of what should an `extension create` command do:

### Option 1: local scaffolding only

- User inputs: extension name
- Creates a new local git repo for the extension
- Generates a new executable file `gh-my-extension`
- [Optional] installs the new extension locally?
- Prints instructions on what should the user do next - e.g. how to publish the extension using `gh repo create`

Pros:
- User can learn & experiment with extensions locally without publishing evidence of them doing so
- Simpler implemenation

Cons:
- Publishing left as an exercise to the user

Personally I'm leaning towards this option.

### Option 2: remote repo for the extension + local checkout

- User inputs: extension name, repo visibility (e.g. public vs. private), optional org name
- Creates a new repository for the extension
- Clones the new repository locally
- Renames the cloned `gh-extension` executable to `gh-my-extension`

Pros:
- Extension already published
- Gives us greater control over creating the repository - e.g. we could apply the `gh-extension` repo topic

Cons:
- User has to choose publishing options before they've written any extension implementation
- gh doesn't offer a repo delete option for people who want to undo an `extension create`
- `extension create` has to replicate significant portion of logic from `repo create`

review_comments: Nice going naming the iteration variable here! 👍

Just had another thought: should this say `Create a new extension locally` so that it's clear that whatever will be created, it's only on your machine?

It can be either here or in the `Long` description. Or maybe it's not necessary. Just an idea!

Just had a thought: Windows doesn't have a concept of executable files. When this file gets added to git, will it retain its executable bit? If not, this could be a workaround on Windows that we could execute locally as part of `create`:
```
git add file_name
git update-index --chmod=+x file_name
```

I asked @vilmibm to help me check on this and the file created was executable on Windows. I don't know if @vilmibm confirmed that when it was added to git it maintained the executable property though.

This is unfortunately the trickiest part of publishing an extension on Windows, so if it turns out that it's needed, I would vote to add the `git add && update-index` calls on Windows (or across every platform for simplicity—it would be a no-op on other platforms anyway!)
